html:
The Burmese, or Bamar, are the largest people of Myanmar, speaking a language of the Sino-Tibetan family. The map draws a "Burmese" area in the hills and valleys of upper Burma and the lands toward Yunnan for 1500, 1000 and 700 BCE, a label that runs far ahead of the history.

Little is known of who lived there in those centuries. Archaeology shows rice farming villages and, from about 1500 BCE, bronze working in the Irrawaddy valley. Speakers of Tibeto-Burman languages were spreading south from the eastern Himalayas and southwest China, but the Bamar themselves are thought to have arrived in the Irrawaddy valley only in the 800s CE, probably from the area of the Nanzhao kingdom.

Before them the valley belonged to the Pyu city-states and to the Mon in the south. The Bamar founded Pagan, whose kings united the valley in the 1000s and adopted Theravada Buddhism. Later Burmese kingdoms grew from that base.
